chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

concepts.name: Genesis of periodic classification
concepts.summary: Early attempts to order elements by atomic weight: Döbereiner's triads and Newlands' Law of Octaves.

concepts.name: Mendeleev's Periodic Law
concepts.summary: Properties as a periodic function of atomic weight, with gaps left for undiscovered elements.

concepts.name: Modern Periodic Law
concepts.summary: Properties are a periodic function of atomic number, not atomic weight.

concepts.name: Periods and groups
concepts.summary: The long form: horizontal periods set by principal quantum number, vertical groups by outer configuration.

concepts.name: Nomenclature of elements with Z > 100
concepts.summary: IUPAC systematic names built from numerical roots until a discovery is confirmed.

concepts.name: Electronic configuration and periods
concepts.summary: Why each period has the length it does, from the orbitals filled in it.

concepts.name: s-, p-, d- and f-blocks
concepts.summary: Elements classified by the type of orbital receiving the last electron.

concepts.name: Position of hydrogen
concepts.summary: Why hydrogen resists placement in either group 1 or group 17.

concepts.name: Metals, non-metals and metalloids
concepts.summary: The broad division and how metallic character varies across and down the table.

concepts.name: Atomic radius
concepts.summary: How atomic size is defined and why it shrinks across a period and grows down a group.

concepts.name: Ionic radius
concepts.summary: Why cations are smaller and anions larger than the parent atom, and isoelectronic comparisons.

concepts.name: Ionization enthalpy
concepts.summary: The energy to remove an electron, its trends, and the two places the trend breaks.

concepts.name: Electron gain enthalpy
concepts.summary: The enthalpy change on adding an electron, and why the second-period anomaly exists.

concepts.name: Electronegativity
concepts.summary: The tendency of a bonded atom to attract shared electrons, on the Pauling scale.

concepts.name: Valence and oxidation state
concepts.summary: Predicting combining capacity from the number of outermost electrons.

facts: genesis-of-periodic-classification
In a Döbereiner triad the middle element's atomic weight is about halfway between the other two
Its properties are also intermediate between the other two members
genesis-of-periodic-classification
Newlands' Law of Octaves held only for elements up to calcium
Newlands received the Davy Medal from the Royal Society in 1887 for the work
mendeleev-periodic-law
Mendeleev arranged elements by increasing atomic weight so that similar properties fell in the same vertical column
He placed elements in horizontal rows and vertical columns; his scheme was more elaborate than Lothar Meyer's
mendeleev-periodic-law
Mendeleev ignored strict atomic-weight order where it conflicted with grouping by property
He assumed the atomic-weight measurements might be incorrect
mendeleev-periodic-law
Mendeleev left gaps for elements he predicted were undiscovered
Gallium and germanium were both unknown when the table was published
modern-periodic-law
The physical and chemical properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers
This is the Modern Periodic Law, a modification of Mendeleev's law
modern-periodic-law
Atomic number equals the nuclear charge, the number of protons, and the number of electrons in a neutral atom
This is what makes quantum numbers and electronic configuration explain periodicity
structure-of-the-periodic-table
Horizontal rows are called periods and vertical columns are called groups
Mendeleev called the rows series
structure-of-the-periodic-table
The period number equals the highest principal quantum number n of the elements in that period
structure-of-the-periodic-table
Period lengths are 2, 8, 8, 18, 18 and 32 elements
The seventh period is incomplete and would theoretically also hold 32
structure-of-the-periodic-table
The 14 lanthanoids and 14 actinoids are placed in separate panels below the main table
They belong to the sixth and seventh periods respectively
nomenclature-above-100
Elements with Z above 100 receive a systematic IUPAC name derived from numerical roots until the discovery is confirmed
The temporary symbol has three letters
electronic-configuration-and-periods
The first period has two elements, hydrogen (1s¹) and helium (1s²)
It completes the first shell, K
electronic-configuration-and-periods
The fourth period begins at potassium filling 4s, and 3d fills before 4p
3d becomes energetically favourable before 4p
electronic-configuration-and-periods
The sixth period holds 32 elements, filling 6s, 4f, 5d and 6p in that order
blocks-of-the-periodic-table
Elements are classified into s-, p-, d- and f-blocks by the type of orbital being filled
blocks-of-the-periodic-table
s-block elements are groups 1 and 2, with outermost configuration ns¹ and ns²
Group 1 are the alkali metals, group 2 the alkaline earth metals
blocks-of-the-periodic-table
s-block elements lose their outermost electrons readily to form 1+ or 2+ ions
They have low ionization enthalpies; metallic character and reactivity increase down the group
blocks-of-the-periodic-table
p-block elements are groups 13 to 18, with outermost configuration from ns²np¹ to ns²np⁶
With the s-block they form the representative or main group elements
blocks-of-the-periodic-table
d-block elements are groups 3 to 12 and are characterised by filling of inner d orbitals
They are the transition elements
blocks-of-the-periodic-table
f-block elements have outer configuration (n-2)f¹⁻¹⁴ (n-1)d⁰⁻¹ns²
Lanthanoids run Ce(58) to Lu(71); actinoids Th(90) to Lr(103)
blocks-of-the-periodic-table
Actinoid elements are radioactive and their chemistry is more complicated than the lanthanoids
They show a larger number of possible oxidation states
position-of-hydrogen
Hydrogen has one s-electron so it can sit in group 1, but can also gain an electron like a group 17 halogen
Because it is a special case it is placed separately at the top of the table
metals-nonmetals-metalloids
Metals comprise more than 78% of all known elements and appear on the left side of the table
They are malleable and ductile
metals-nonmetals-metalloids
Metallic character increases down a group and non-metallic character increases left to right across a period
The change is gradual, marked by a zig-zag line, with metalloids such as silicon along it
atomic-radius
Atomic size cannot be measured directly because the electron cloud has no sharp boundary
atomic-radius
Covalent radius is half the internuclear distance in a molecule; the Cl₂ bond distance is 198 pm giving chlorine a radius of 99 pm
Metallic radius is half the internuclear distance between metal cores in the crystal
atomic-radius
Atomic radius of second-period elements falls from Li 152 pm to F 64 pm
Third period falls from Na 186 pm to Cl 99 pm
atomic-radius
Atomic size generally decreases across a period
Increasing nuclear charge pulls the electrons of the same energy level closer
atomic-radius
Atomic size increases down a group because n increases and inner electrons shield the outer ones
Shielding outweighs the increase in nuclear charge
ionic-radius
A cation is smaller than its parent atom and an anion is larger
An added electron increases electron-electron repulsion and lowers effective nuclear charge
ionic-radius
The fluoride ion F⁻ has a radius of 136 pm
ionic-radius
Among isoelectronic species the one with the larger positive nuclear charge has the smaller radius
ionization-enthalpy
The first ionization enthalpy is the enthalpy change for X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻
Expressed in kJ mol⁻¹
ionization-enthalpy
The second ionization enthalpy is always higher than the first
Removing an electron from a positive ion is harder than from a neutral atom
ionization-enthalpy
Ionization enthalpy is governed by attraction to the nucleus and repulsion between electrons
Core electrons shield the valence electron, so effective nuclear charge is less than the actual charge
ionization-enthalpy
Boron has a lower first ionization enthalpy than beryllium
Beryllium loses a 2s electron while boron loses a more shielded, less penetrating 2p electron
ionization-enthalpy
Oxygen has a lower first ionization enthalpy than nitrogen
Nitrogen's three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals by Hund's rule; oxygen must pair two in one orbital, adding repulsion
electron-gain-enthalpy
Group 17 halogens have very high negative electron gain enthalpies
Adding an electron gives them a stable noble gas configuration
electron-gain-enthalpy
Noble gases have large positive electron gain enthalpies
The added electron must enter the next higher principal quantum level
electron-gain-enthalpy
Electron gain enthalpy generally becomes more negative across a period
Effective nuclear charge rises left to right, so a smaller atom accepts an electron more readily
electron-gain-enthalpy
Chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine
The electron added to fluorine enters the small n = 2 level and suffers significant repulsion
electronegativity
Pauling assigned fluorine a value of 4.0, the highest, in 1922
The Pauling scale is the most widely used
electronegativity
Electronegativity of an element is not constant and depends on the element it is bonded to
electronegativity
Electronegativity increases as atomic radius decreases across a period
Attraction between valence electrons and nucleus rises as the radius falls
electronegativity
Electronegativity is directly related to non-metallic character and inversely related to metallic character
valence-and-oxidation-state
Valence of a representative element equals the number of outermost electrons, or eight minus that number
The term oxidation state is now frequently used for valence
valence-and-oxidation-state
In OF₂ oxygen shows oxidation state +2; in Na₂O it shows −2
Oxygen (2s²2p⁴) shares two electrons with fluorine but accepts two from sodium

methods.name: Ordering elements by metallic character
methods.trigger: A list of elements to arrange by metallic or non-metallic character
steps: Locate each element's group and period
Apply: metallic character increases down a group
Apply: metallic character decreases left to right across a period
methods.common_error: Reading the period trend the wrong way round — metallic character falls, not rises, across a period

methods.name: Ranking isoelectronic species by size
methods.trigger: Several ions and atoms with the same electron count, to be ordered by radius
steps: Write the nuclear charge (Z) of each
Larger positive nuclear charge pulls the same electron cloud tighter, so radius falls as Z rises
Order from lowest Z (largest) to highest Z (smallest)
methods.common_error: Ranking by the size of the charge on the ion rather than by nuclear charge

methods.name: Predicting a compound's formula from group valences
methods.trigger: Two elements given, asked for the formula they would form
steps: Read off valence: outermost electrons, or eight minus that
Cross the valences to balance combining capacity
methods.common_error: Using the group number directly as the valence for groups 15 to 17 instead of eight minus the outer electrons

methods.name: Placing an element from its atomic number
methods.trigger: An atomic number given, asked for group, block or configuration
steps: Build the electronic configuration by the aufbau order
The highest n gives the period
The orbital receiving the last electron gives the block
Outer electron count gives the group
methods.common_error: Forgetting that 3d fills before 4p, which shifts every fourth-period placement

connections: Periodicity follows from electronic configuration, which is why ordering by atomic number works where atomic weight failed.
A smaller radius holds the valence electron more tightly, so ionization enthalpy rises as radius falls.
Electronegativity rises as atomic radius falls, because the nucleus attracts bonded electrons more strongly.
One measures the cost of losing an electron, the other the enthalpy change on gaining one; both are governed by effective nuclear charge and shielding.
The block an element belongs to is fixed by the orbital being filled, which also fixes its group.
Electronegativity is directly related to non-metallic character and inversely to metallic character.
Ionic radii are understood as departures from the parent atomic radius when electrons are lost or gained.
misconceptions: Ionization enthalpy rises steadily across a period with no exceptions
The general trend is upward, so the dips at boron and oxygen look like errors rather than consequences of orbital type and electron pairing
Boron must have a higher ionization enthalpy than beryllium because it has a higher nuclear charge
Nuclear charge does rise, but the electron removed from boron is a less penetrating 2p electron that is better shielded
Fluorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy because it is the most electronegative element
Electronegativity and electron gain enthalpy are different quantities; fluorine's small n = 2 shell makes the added electron suffer more repulsion than in chlorine
Atomic radius can be measured directly for a single atom
Radii are quoted as precise numbers in tables, which hides that they are derived from internuclear distances because the electron cloud has no boundary
A cation is larger than its parent atom because it has more protons than electrons
Charge is associated with strength, but losing an electron reduces repulsion and lets the nucleus pull the rest in, making the cation smaller
The periodic table is ordered by atomic weight
Mendeleev's original law used atomic weight and the tables look similar, but the modern law is a function of atomic number
